Q134285876.summary: Within an acanthus border, Christ hangs on the cross beneath the INRI title, his head inclined and his feet resting on a footrest. The Virgin raises her hands in sorrow at the left, and John, holding a book, stands at the right. The quiet, balanced composition reflects the restrained dignity of German ivory carving in the 11th century.
facts: The pairing of the Virgin and John beneath the cross recalls Christ's words entrusting his mother to the beloved disciple.
Q134285876.notes: Little published information was found beyond Wikidata and the Commons file (Germany, 11th century, ivory).
Q134285876.original_title: Christus am Kreuz zwischen Maria und Johannes

cur:legends-santo-rostro-jaen.summary: Within a frame blazing with gems, a pale cloth bears the faint face of Christ, its outline ending below in a pointed beard. Jaén venerates this image, the Santo Rostro, as one of the imprints left on the veil with which Veronica wiped Christ's face on the way to Calvary; the present cathedral was conceived as its sanctuary. No scientific study of its date is available, and it is best understood as a medieval vera icon long honoured by the city.
cur:legends-santo-rostro-jaen.scripture: Luke 23:26–31 (theme: the way to Calvary; the Veronica episode is not in the Gospels)
facts: Its jewelled frame was made in 1731 by the Córdoba silversmith José Francisco de Valderrama for Bishop Rodrigo Marín Rubio, set with 191 rubies, 193 diamonds and 210 emeralds.
The relic is kept in a strongbox behind the high altar, covered by a painted panel by Sebastián Martínez showing two angels holding the veil, and is exposed for veneration every Friday.
The balconies of the cathedral's Baroque façade were used to display the Santo Rostro to bless the surrounding land and people.
cur:legends-santo-rostro-jaen.notes: The date of the image itself is not established in any source consulted; y=1370 reflects its documented presence in the cathedral under Bishop Nicolás de Biedma (1368–1383), who according to es.wikipedia secured its return after it had been taken to Seville by Ferdinand III. Image is small (317 px wide). The collection's commons:124208725 shows the retable that houses it (with the Virgen de la Antigua), a different photograph and focus.

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-chris.summary: Within a niche framed by bands of colour, a bearded Christ holding a jewelled book stands at the centre between two haloed saints, shown half-length against a gold ground. The frontal, solemn figures, with large dark eyes and strongly outlined features, are typical of the mosaic style of Paschal I's Rome.
facts: The Chapel of Saint Zeno was built by Pope Paschal I (817–824) as a funerary chapel for his mother, Theodora; its walls and vault are almost entirely clad in gold-ground mosaic.
Paschal I's mosaics belong to the Carolingian-era revival in Rome, when the pope also translated many martyrs' relics from the catacombs into the city's churches.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Basilica of Saint Praxedes (Rome) - Jesus Christ between two saints mosaic

cur:monumental-santa-prassede-zeno-chris.notes: The flanking saints are identified variously; the Flickr source names them as Paschal and Valentinus, Commons also suggests Valentinus and Zeno.

cur:monumental2-tokali-christ-enthroned.summary: Christ sits frontally on a high-backed jewelled throne with a cushion, a large cross-inscribed halo behind his head, holding a richly bound Gospel book on his knee and raising his right hand in blessing. Much of the paint of the face and mantle has worn away, but the monumental pose of the Ruler of All remains clear.
facts: Enthroned images of Christ holding the Gospel book were often placed in apses or flanked by the Virgin and John the Baptist in a Deesis, as intercession for the faithful.
cur:monumental2-tokali-christ-enthroned.notes: The photograph is labelled only 'Christ Pantocrator scene'; its exact position within Tokalı Kilise (Old or New Church) was not verified, so a general 10th-century date is given.

walters:W.432.63V.summary: In the upper miniature, Christ stands bound on a raised, columned porch beside Pilate, who gestures toward the crowd below; the people shout and raise their arms, demanding Barabbas instead. In the lower one, Christ, stripped and covered with wounds, is beaten by two tormentors, one with a bundle of birch rods, while in the background figures press the crown of thorns onto his head. The two images follow the Gospel text between them, from 'Non hunc sed Barabbam' to the scourging and crowning.
facts: The page carries two miniatures, 9 and 5 lines high, illustrating John 18:38–40 and John 19:1–16.
The prayer book was made in Leiden in the first quarter of the 16th century.

links.label: The Digital Walters: Prayer Book with Passages from the Gospels (W.432)

walters:W.432.63V.notes: Origin in Leiden and the date 1500–1525 follow the Walters manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters). The worklist year (800) was a parsing error for '1st quarter 16th century'. The Walters title 'The Jews Release Barabbas Instead of Christ' is replaced with a more neutral descriptive title.

Q4536026.summary: On the banks of the Jordan, John the Baptist points to a small, solitary figure descending from the hills: the Messiah approaching a crowd that has not yet recognized him. Ivanov devoted twenty years in Rome to this vast canvas, seeking to capture the single instant when humanity first beholds its Saviour, and it became a landmark of Russian religious art.
facts: The painting measures 5.4 by 7.5 metres, and Ivanov made hundreds of preparatory sketches and studies of landscapes, figures and heads for it.
Ivanov's friend, the writer Nikolai Gogol, is traditionally said to appear in the crowd as the figure nearest to Christ, though some scholars regard this as a myth.
Ivanov brought the canvas to St Petersburg in 1858 and died of cholera only weeks later; word that Tsar Alexander II would buy the work arrived hours after his death.
Ivanov resisted bringing Christ forward: he appears small and far off on the hillside, as John the Baptist would have seen him, so the viewer, like the crowd, must look for him.

Q79961.summary: Standing with open arms on the summit of Corcovado, about 700 metres above Rio de Janeiro, Christ the Redeemer has become one of the most recognised images of Christ in the world. Its simple, streamlined Art Deco form makes it readable from the city far below, and the outstretched arms form both a cross and a gesture of embrace. It was dedicated on 12 October 1931 and has become a symbol of Brazil itself.
facts: The statue is about 30 metres tall on an 8-metre pedestal, and its arms span roughly 28 metres.
Its reinforced-concrete frame is covered with a mosaic of thousands of small triangular soapstone tiles, a stone chosen for its durability and ease of working.
It was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007, and it is regularly struck by lightning: a 2014 strike dislodged a finger on the right hand.
